newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: C&W now seen making the calls at Optus.
newsitem.headline: C&W now seen making the calls at Optus.

text.p: British telephone carrier Cable and Wireless Plc (C&W) had increased its influence at Australia's Optus Communications Pty Ltd after the appointment last week of one of its executives to head Optus, analysts said.

Optus, Australia's second biggest telecommunications carrier, last Friday appointed Peter Howell-Davies as its chief executive officer. He replaced Ziggy Switkowski, who resigned after only one year on the job.
The boardroom manoeuvres were also likely to push the long-awaited share offer of Optus back to 1998, analysts said.

Howell-Davies, former chief executive of C&W's British telephony unit Mercury, has the initial task of fixing problems with the cable television offshoot Optus Vision and then work on the float, which has lukewarm support among some investors.

The swift appointment of Howell-Davies was part of a wider move by the British telecom group to exert more influence over Optus, with talk that it might buy the 24.5 percent stake held in Optus by BellSouth Corp, analyst said.
"It looks like there is a move on the BellSouth shareholding by Cable and Wireless," said one Sydney-based telecom analyst, who asked not to be named.

C&W holds 24.5 percent of Optus and under foreign ownership rules would be able to raise its Optus stake to 49 percent, analysts said. C&W would not be able to buy any of the shares held by Australian shareholders, who control 51 percent.

"BellSouth are more interested in their South American interests and that is mainly their international focus. Also, they are not happy with the Optus Vision strategy, they felt it should have been liquidated," the Sydney analyst said.
Optus bought out minority shareholders in its cable television unit Optus Vision earlier this year after lengthy litigation with former Optus Vision shareholders.

The loss-making Optus Vision is likely to pull the Optus group into a loss for the current financial year as the cost of its cable network rollout is bleeding red ink over the group's balance sheet, analysts said.

The Optus Vision merger and Optus' future strategy on Australia's pay television split the company's board and was seen as the major reason for Switkowski's exit. He wanted Optus to stay in pay tv, analysts said.
Analysts said the board members that wanted Optus to get out of pay TV content and focus on the delivery side of the business seems to have won the boardroom battle for now.
"Certainly telephone companies have a real role to play in providing the wires and cables to deliver pay tv," said Mark Smeaton, telecommunications analyst at Macquarie Equities.
"The notion that telephone companies can be actively involved in the provision of pay TV content is, I think, presently flawed," Smeaton told Reuters.

Analysts said Howell-Davies had the right creditionals for combining telephony and cable TV companies, citing the merger this year between Mercury with three cable TV companies to create Cable & Wireless Communications Plc (CWC).

"I guess you could see that (CWC) as an emerging model to what might happen here, where you have telephone companies in charge of infrastructure and telephony, (but) they don't actually own any of the pay tv content," Macquarie's Smeaton said.

Last month, C&W sold a 5.5 percent stake worth US$1.2 billion in Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd to state-owned China Telecom, which analysts said may lead to a further sell down in Hong Kong Telecom.
"In Hong Kong they might be forced to sell down to a minority holding, if so, they will look to aggressively look to boost their presence elsewhere," Smeaton said.

Optus' biggest shareholder, transport and health care group Mayne Nickless Ltd is eager to sell its 24.9 percent stake. The balance of the shares, which are not owned by C&W or BellSouth, are in the hands of Australian institutions.
-- Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
